claims.text: Thermal exposure of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy causes Mg diffusion, segregation, and precipitation as Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Selective Mg-rich precipitation modifies the local distribution of protective elements such as Ti and Zn.
Changes in the surface oxide film caused by selective precipitation change both aqueous corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering can produce a fine, metastable mixture of solid solutions and incipient intermetallic compounds in the proposed alloy.
The proposed alloy has an overall density below 6 g/cm3.
Rapid quenching after thermal exposure retains the original metastable state relative to thermal aging.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates nucleate preferentially at grain boundaries or phase interfaces.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates alter local elemental distributions and consequently influence surface-oxide formation and properties.
The non-equilibrium state enables rapid Mg diffusion during thermal exposure.
Thermally formed intermetallics disrupt homogeneous oxidation and produce a mixed oxide layer containing protective TiO2 or ZnO near the intermetallics.
A heterogeneous mixed oxide scale can enhance or compromise corrosion passivation and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Relative to the as-quenched baseline, thermal aging produces measurable differences in oxide-scale composition or thickness.
Relative to the as-quenched baseline, thermal aging produces a measurable shift in corrosion current density.
Whether performance improves or degrades depends on the passivating effectiveness of the newly formed mixed oxide structure.
The as-sintered or rapidly quenched baseline has a more homogeneous microstructure and oxide layer before substantial Mg segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies only to sub-6 g/cm3 compositions maintained as metastable phase mixtures and exposed to controlled oxidizing or aqueous chloride environments.
Ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered equimolar MgTiZn contains Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25 intermetallic phases.
Ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered Mg4TiZn has a predominantly Mg-rich phase.
MgTiZn forms a TiO2-rich surface film that was attributed to enhanced passivation and lower corrosion current density.
In 0.1 M NaCl, MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn exhibited corrosion current densities of 3.65 ± 0.65 and 4.58 ± 1.64 µA/cm2, respectively.

contradictions.description: Thermal exposure is asserted to activate diffusion and precipitation, yet the proposed control is quenched only after the same elevated-temperature exposure and is described as preserving the original metastable microstructure. Without a shorter hold or other distinction before quenching, that control may undergo the very transformation it is intended to suppress.
